abstract: Background Recent studies focus on the genetic and physiological characteristics of the plains Han, plateau Han, and Tibetan populations. However, systematic studies on the differences in metabolic and microbial communities in high-altitude environments remain limited. Results This study profiled metabolomes and microbiomes in plain Han, plateau Han, and Tibetan populations. Differential analysis revealed 30 metabolites and notable alterations in microbial community composition between plain Han and plateau Han. Prevotella , Streptococcus , and Ruminococcus , mainly participating in purine metabolism, were enriched in the plateau Han population. Bacteroidota and Firmicutes were the primary differential bacterial phyla indicating adaptive alternatives, particularly in steroid metabolism. Thirty-four distinct metabolites were identified between plateau Han and Tibetan individuals, including significant lipids such as ceramide, triglycerides (TG), and phosphatidylethanolamine (PE). These lipids and metabolites were integrally involved in energy metabolism and inflammatory pathways, highlighting the importance of high-altitude environments for metabolic health. Conclusions This study identified significant associations between metabolic, lipid, and microbial differences and altitude-induced physiological variation, illustrating population adaptations to extreme environments. Our systematic comparative analysis improves our understanding of high-altitude adaptability, underlining the importance of integrating metabolic and microbiological analyses and facilitating future research on associated disorders. Supplementary Information The online version contains supplementary material available at 10.1186/s12915-025-02430-5.

Methods
Study cohort
We carefully designed the experiment and recruitment criteria, and recruited a total of 349 healthy Han Chinese and Tibetan Chinese residents, of which 94 Han Chinese lived in the plain at an average altitude of 1200 m and had never been to the plateau; 162 Han Chinese and 93 Tibetans lived in the plateau at an average altitude of 4300 m, and the Han Chinese had been working in the plateau for more than 3 months, and this was their first time going there. 93 Tibetans had always lived on the plateau and had never been to the plain. All the samples of the plain-living population were collected on the plain, and all the samples of the plateau-living population were collected on the plateau. The Han and Tibetan populations on the plateau have roughly similar diets and lifestyles; they live in the same cafeteria and eat traditional Chinese food in the same cafeteria, and the plain populations have similar lifestyles and diets to those on the plateau. Thus, this design largely eliminated some confounders (diet and lifestyle), with the main factors being ethnicity and altitude differences. All participants were healthy, had no known clinical illnesses, and were not taking medications or receiving any interventions during the plateau. See supplemental data 1 in the supplementary material for raw data statistics.
Collection of blood and fecal samples, biochemistry tests
In the morning when participants were fasting, 8 ml of anticoagulated blood was collected using EDTA-K2, mixed by gentle up and down mixing, centrifuged using a centrifugation speed of 4000 rpm for 10 min, and the supernatant (200 µL) was then transferred into a 1.5-mL centrifuge tube for untargeted metabolomics analysis using LC–MS/MS. Plasma samples were separated and transported to the PLA General Hospital (Beijing, approximately 40 m above sea level) while maintaining − 80 °C temperature throughout transit to ensure sample stability. Two milliliters of plasma were taken for 76 clinical parameters using a hematology analyzer (Roche, USA), and the supernatant was taken for metabolite assays, all of which were performed by Metware Biotechnology (Wuhan, China), and all the blood tests and basic statistical descriptions are detailed in supplemental data 1. Fresh fecal samples were collected using a sterile fecal collector. The middle portion of the sample was then taken using a sterile fecal sampler. Each fecal sample was weighed at approximately 0.2 g and dispensed into a new 1.5-mL centrifuge tube. Each sample collected is transferred to − 80 °C within 20 min for storage.
Sample preparation and extraction
16S rRNA gene sequencing. Fecal specimens were extracted using the standard method of Novogene (Beijing, China), and PCR was performed to amplify the V3–V4 region of the 16S rRNA gene using the 341F/806R primers. We mixed the amplification products with 1 × loading buffer containing SYBR green fluorescent dye in equal volumes, and then prepared sequencing libraries according to the manufacturer’s protocol for the Ion Plus Fragment Library Kit 48rxns from Thermo Scientific (USA). We chose to perform high-throughput sequencing on the Ion S5 XL platform and obtained approximately 400 bp of single-ended raw reads from each sample.
Metabolite assay
In this study, metabolite analysis was performed using the Metware Metabolic Assay System, where liquid samples were first prepared and extracted; hydrophilic compounds were mixed by 20% acetonitrile-methanol internal standard extracts and the supernatant was obtained by centrifugation, whereas hydrophobic compounds were processed by methyl tert-butyl ether (MTBE): MeOH extracts. Then, the hydrophilic and hydrophobic compounds were analyzed separately by UPLC technique, where the hydrophilic compounds were analyzed by two UPLC conditions including T3 and Amide, and the hydrophobic compounds were analyzed by UPLC conditions involving a C30 column. Finally, the hydrophilic and hydrophobic compounds were analyzed by ESI-Q TRAP-MS/MS mass spectrometry system, and the metabolite data were obtained by using LIT and QQQ scanning modes, which provided an effective means of revealing the in-depth composition and abundance of metabolites in the samples.
Analytical methods
Analysis of clinical indicators
We used the shapiro.test function in the
R
statistical package, which was used to perform the Shapiro–Wilk normality test on the clinical indicator data, with the
p
-value cutoff set at 0.05. To compare the differences in normally distributed variables between the two groups, we used an independent
t
-test. For the assessment of differences between non-normally distributed data, we instead chose the Wilcoxon test. To correct for multiple comparisons, we applied the Benjamini–Hochberg procedure to control the false discovery rate (FDR). This approach was used to adjust p-values for all tests conducted in the study to minimize the risk of Type I errors due to multiple testing. The
p
-values were adjusted using the Benjamini–Hochberg procedure with a false discovery rate threshold of 0.05.
Identification of differential metabolites
We applied the Wilcoxon test using the Wilcox.test function in the R package, with the
p
-value set to 0.05 to identify metabolites showing significant differences between groups. In addition, we also relied on the RandomForest method, which was performed by the “randomForest” function in the R package “randomForest” to build the model. The model performance was evaluated with the help of the predict function for the test dataset and the multiclass.roc function to calculate the AUC value to evaluate the model performance. To identify the most influential metabolites, we calculated the importance of model variables and selected the top 30 metabolites based on their variable importance scores. In addition, we used the OPLS-DA method and grouped principal component analysis, which was performed using the R package “ropls”. In the determination of significantly different metabolites, we relied on the criteria VIP ≥ 1 and absolute Log2FC ≥ 1. These thresholds were chosen as they are widely used in metabolomics studies to identify variables with the highest discrimination power between groups. Prior to the application of the above methods, we performed logarithmic transformation (log2) on all metabolic data. For cluster analysis, we used the R package “ComplexHeatmap” for cluster analysis of samples and differential metabolites, and the R package “glasso” for the analysis of differential metabolites and clinical indicators.
Microbiome analysis
For high-throughput sequencing data analysis, we used the R package DADA2. Sequences were demultiplexed, and non-biological nucleotides (primers, adapters) were removed using cutadapt (v5.1). Low-quality bases were filtered and corrected, and ASVs were generated using DADA2 (v1.26), which includes sequence dereplication, error correction, and chimera removal. Taxonomy was assigned using the assignTaxonomy function in DADA2, which employs a naive Bayesian classifier based on
k
-mer frequency to assign taxonomic affiliations across multiple taxonomic ranks. The sequences were compared to the SILVA v138.2 database, and only bacterial ASVs were retained for downstream analysis. On this basis, we retained only bacterial sequence variants (ASVs) and filtered out sequences from other domains. Compositional and functional analysis of the microbiome was performed using the R package “phyloseq,” involving filtering of low-frequency sequence variants, removal of unclassified phyla, and normalization of ASV abundance. At the same time, we performed α-diversity analysis and β-diversity analysis based on diversity indices such as Chao1, Shannon, Simpson, and ACE, respectively, and also used β-diversity analysis based on Unweighted-UniFrac distance. For microbiome function analysis, we used the PiCRUST2 software to predict microbiome functions and to estimate the involvement of microorganisms in different functional pathways. For differential abundance analysis of microbiome functions, we used the R software packages “ggpicrust2” and “MaAsLin2” to reveal the correlation between microbiome and clinical data.
KEGG annotation and enrichment analysis
To annotate the metabolites identified by the 3 methods, we used the KEGG Compound database. Subsequently, we mapped the annotated metabolites to the KEGG Pathway database to identify significantly enriched pathways; we applied the
p
-value of the hypergeometric test. This step aims to perform pathway enrichment analysis for a given list of metabolites.

body:
Background
The plateau is a unique ecosystem characterized by extreme cold, low oxygen levels, and intense ultraviolet radiation, which profoundly impact human physiology [
1
]. The distinct hypoxic environment and extreme climatic conditions promote adaptive metabolic changes in the high-altitude population. Researchers worldwide have undertaken substantial studies in this field, revealing the effects of high-altitude environments on human metabolism as well as potential molecular mechanisms [
2
,
3
]. Furthermore, hypoxic and extreme cold conditions can cause intestinal mucosal ischemia and gut barrier injury, resulting in a microbiota imbalance. Long-term residence at high altitudes can induce adaptive changes in the gut microbiome composition [
4
–
6
]. Therefore, studying the interrelated regulation of metabolism and microbiota in high-altitude populations is crucial for scientific research, medical exploration, and human health.
Metabolomic studies primarily focus on elucidating the intricate interactions between metabolic pathways, networks, and metabolites within living organisms. These studies provide a comprehensive understanding of dynamic metabolic changes and their correlations with physiological states and disease progression [
6
]. It is critical for plateau metabolomic studies to investigate the metabolic adaptation mechanisms that affect health and survival in high-altitude populations exposed to extreme environments such as hypoxia, low air pressure, and cold [
7
]. Studies have shown that the genetic adaptation to high altitude in Tibetans was related to oxygen delivery regulation and cellular metabolism alterations to optimize oxygen utilization [
8
]. High-throughput proteomics and metabolomics analyses confirmed altered tissue metabolism in Tibetan populations at high altitude. Genome scans of high-altitude Tibetan populations found that peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor alpha (PPARA) regulated cellular energy metabolism in the heart, skeletal muscle, and liver [
8
]. Genetic variation shifted fatty acid oxidation toward more efficient oxygen metabolism while decreasing ATP requirements. Non-Tibetans acclimated to high altitude exhibit inhibition of oxidative metabolism in the heart and skeletal muscle, including reduced fatty acid oxidation (FAO) capacity and increased glycolysis [
9
]. When plain populations entered high altitudes, their erythrocytes underwent metabolic reprogramming that affected energy, amino acid, and nucleotide metabolisms, which in turn impacted physiological functions such as oxygen transport [
10
]. As hypoxia intensified, the anaerobic metabolism of brain cells increased, ATP production decreased, the sodium pump function of the brain cell membrane impaired, intracellular sodium and water retention occurred, and plateau cerebral edema developed [
11
,
12
]. However, most previous studies focused on single metabolomic analyses and did not incorporate multi-omics data to investigate metabolic adaptation at high altitudes. Consequently, multi-omics analyses are essential to comprehensively understand high-altitude metabolic adaptation mechanisms in diverse populations.
Growing evidence suggested that variations in microbial composition may greatly contribute to metabolic differences. Gut microbes play an important role in human metabolism, influencing food degradation, energy absorption, and metabolite production [
13
]. As a result, understanding how altitude and ethnicity affect gut microbiota and their interactions with host metabolism holds considerable promise for unraveling the intricate network of factors that regulate human health [
14
,
15
]. Animal studies showed that hypoxia exposure at different altitudes and durations altered the diversity and structure of the rat gut microbial community [
16
]. In hypobaric hypoxia chamber mice, gut microbiome-targeted feeding can alleviate pathologic cardiac hypertrophy, gut microbiota dysbiosis, and metabolic disturbances in the gut and plasma [
17
]. Therefore, gut microbiota composition may contribute to high-altitude-associated diseases and serve as a therapeutic target.
The gut microbiota of high-altitude individuals has been extensively studied. Jia’s study found that the general characteristics and clinical indicators of Han Chinese gut microbiota became increasingly similar to Tibetan ones with the prolongation of the plateau living time. The intestinal flora of Han Chinese who returned to the plain for 3 months was identical to that of the plateau Han Chinese but different from plain Han Chinese. The low-oxygen environment can rapidly and persistently affect the human intestinal microbiota and blood clinical indexes [
18
]. Nevertheless, these studies have mostly focused on certain microbial taxa. Since gut microbiota significantly impacts metabolism, a thorough analysis of gut microbiota composition and its metabolic products is necessary to properly comprehend the potential effects of high-altitude environments on human health. While genetic analysis has revealed potential metabolic mechanisms conferring hypoxia tolerance in humans and other species in high-altitude regions, high-throughput techniques like proteomics, metabolomics, and metagenomics have untapped potential for elucidating the functional consequences of genetic signals [
9
].
Through a comprehensive study of various ethnic groups, including Han Chinese and Tibetans, at different altitudes, we combined clinical indicators, metabolomics analysis, and microbial community profiling to uncover these complex relationships between ethnicity, environment, metabolic factors, and microbiota. The present study offers new perspectives in personalized health management and disease prevention, advancing our understanding of the interplay between metabolism, environment, and genetics.
Results
The blood and fecal samples from 349 participants, including healthy participants from the Chinese Han and Tibetan individuals who lived in both plain and plateau areas, were collected. The participants consisted of 94 Han inhabitants from the plain region, 162 Han people from the plateau region, and 93 Tibetan residents. All participants were male; baseline characteristics, including age, height, and weight, were compared across the three groups, with no significant differences observed (Supplementary Table 1). A total of 630 broad-target metabolites, 476 lipid metabolites, and microbiome data with 663 ASV, 998 genera, 40 classes, and 48 blood clinical indicators were identified among all participants (Fig.
1
A).

A

B

C
The trend of clinical indicators in different groups
Ethnic and altitude differences significantly influence clinical indicators
To investigate the ethnic and altitude differences, we divided the participants into two groups: plain Han vs. plateau Han (a) and plateau Han vs. plateau Tibetan (b) (Fig.
1
B). Forty-eight indicators were measured and categorized into seven groups: hormones, metabolic indicators, infectious disease markers, immuno-inflammation, liver function, circulatory system, and tumor markers.
Plain Han shared 11 indicators vs. plateau Han and plateau Han vs. plateau Tibetan comparisons, while 18 and 11 indicators were unique to each comparison, respectively (Fig.
1
B). Compared to the plain Han population, the plateau Han population exhibited higher levels of lipase, insulin, glucose, and uric acid and lower levels of pancreatic amylase, high-density lipoprotein, urea, and apolipoprotein A1, with notable decreases in tumor markers such as Free Prostate Specific Antigen (FPSA), human epitope protein 4, and cancer antigen 19.9 (Fig.
1
C). In comparison to the Tibetan population, the plateau Han population showed elevated glucose levels but decreased levels of apolipoprotein A1, high-density lipoprotein, cholesterol, pancreatic amylase, and urea (Fig.
1
C). Hormonal analysis indicated higher testosterone, lower free triiodothyronine and triiodothyronine levels, and higher progesterone and cortisol (Fig.
1
C). These findings indicate that plateau Han and Tibetan populations significantly differ in hormonal and metabolic indicators, indicating adaptive modifications to prolonged low-oxygen conditions. Compared to the plain environment, reduced oxygen pressure in the plateau environment substantially impacts metabolism, immunity, endocrine function, and other physiological characteristics.
Metabolomic differences between ethnic groups and altitudes
To further study the underlying mechanisms of the observed differences in clinical markers, we conducted comprehensive targeted and lipid metabolomics analyses on plasma samples from each participant using ultra performance liquid chromatography high-definition mass spectrometry (UPLC-HDMS). The Wilcoxon test, random forest, and orthogonal partial least squares discriminant analysis (OPLS-DA) methods were employed to identify distinct metabolites between the groups.
In Han people from plain and high-altitude locations, the three approaches identified 16, 21, and 9 distinct metabolites, respectively, with 8 metabolites (4-aminobenzoate,
diallyl sulfide, Dl-2-aminooctanoic acid,
L
-lactic acid, pyrrole-2-carboxylic acid, 2-methylbenzoic acid, estrone, and trans-3-hydroxycotinin shared by all methods. Additionally, 48, 30, and 56 lipid metabolites were detected, with 22 showing consistent variation between samples. The primary distinguishing metabolites included ceramide, S-sulfo-L-cysteine, trigonelline, hypoxanthine-9-β-D-arabinofuranoside, diacylglycerol (DG), TG, and PE, categorized under nucleotide metabolism, organic acid and its derivatives, and triglycerides (Fig.
2
). In comparing Han and Tibetan groups residing in high-altitude regions, 34 shared extensive targets, and 32 lipid metabolites were identified (Supplemental Fig. 1). Key distinguishing metabolites in these groups were DL-2-aminooctanoic acid, deoxycholic acid, hyodeoxycholic acid, guanosine diphosphate (GDP), and TG, which were classified as constitutive androstane receptor (CAR), organic acid and its derivatives, bile acids, and triglycerides. The OPLS-DA analysis results showed significant differences between plain and plateau Han and Tibetan populations (Supplemental Fig. 2). Taken together, these findings demonstrated notable differences in nucleotide, purine, and lipid metabolism between Han groups living in plain and high-altitude environments, and significant disparities in lipid and steroid metabolism between Han and Tibetan populations in high altitude.

A

B

Metabolites and clinical indicator correlations reveal altitude- and ethnicity-related metabolic differences
To thoroughly understand the correlation between clinical indicators and metabolites, lasso analysis was performed on plain Han vs. plateau Han and plateau Han vs. plateau Tibetan groups. Clinical indicators and metabolites showed robust correlations (Supplemental Fig. 3). The plain Han and plateau Han individuals significantly correlated with hypoxanthine-9-β-D-arabinofuranoside and urea, lipid droplet-interacting protein (LDIP), and cancer antigen 724 (CA724) levels (Fig.
3
A and B). Furthermore, fluctuations in ceramide and phosphatidylethanolamine levels were correlated with a reduction in free triiodothyronine (FT3) levels (Fig.
3
C and D). Guanosine diphosphate, a broad-target differential metabolite, correlated significantly with clinical indicators such as blood uric acid, total cholesterol, albumin (ALB), pancreatic amylase (AMY.P), apolipoprotein A (APOA), and insulin 2 in high-altitude Han-Tibetans (Fig.
3
C and D). These findings highlighted significant disparities in purine and lipid metabolism between Han populations at different altitudes, as well as substantial differences in steroid and lipid metabolism between Tibetan and Han populations residing at high altitudes.

A

B

C

KEGG enrichment analysis uncovers key metabolic pathways influenced by altitude and ethnicity
To explore the potential interactions and regulatory mechanisms of distinct metabolites, we conducted a KEGG functional enrichment analysis on the differential metabolites identified in the plain Han vs. plateau Han and plateau Han vs. plateau Tibetan comparisons. We found six enriched common biological pathways for broad-target metabolites and fifteen enriched common pathways for lipid differential metabolites in Han populations living at different altitudes (Fig.
4
). Untargeted metabolites were primarily concentrated in pathways such as purine metabolism, nucleotide metabolism, ovarian steroidogenesis, and the degradation of aromatic compounds (Fig.
4
A). Lipid metabolites were predominantly associated with pathways related to cholesterol metabolism, glyceride metabolism, insulin resistance, lipid metabolism, and atherosclerosis (Fig.
4
B). In the high-altitude environment, four distinct pathways were identified for Han populations and nine for Tibetan populations, relating primarily to cholesterol metabolism, insulin resistance, fat digestion and absorption, lipid metabolism, atherosclerosis, degradation of aromatic compounds, bile secretion, and histidine metabolism (Fig.
4
). These findings suggest that metabolic adaptations to high-altitude environments involve multiple pathways related to lipid and nucleotide metabolism, potentially mediated by interactions with gut microbiota.

Gut microbiota composition and its impact on metabolome differ between altitudes and ethnic groups
To investigate the impact of gut bacteria on the host plasma metabolome, we conducted 16S rRNA sequencing analysis to study the composition and diversity of microbiota of people from different ethnic and altitude groups. LEfSe analysis revealed that
Actinobacteriota
and
Bacteroidota
were the most common bacteria in plain and high-altitude Han populations (Fig.
5
A). We assessed biological diversity among populations in plain and high-altitude regions using α-diversity and β-diversity. PCoA analysis revealed significant gut microbiota diversity variations between plain and high-altitude Han groups (Fig.
5
B). Among all methods, Wilcoxon rank-sum tests showed significant differences in the Shannon index, which indicated species richness and evenness, and the Simpson index, which reflected community evenness (Fig.
5
C). At the genus level, high-altitude Han individuals had much higher abundance of multiple genera, including
Prevotella_9
, but
Subdoligranulum
,
Blautia
, and
Fusicatenibacte
r abundances were dramatically lower (Fig.
5
D, Supplementary Fig. 4D). Therefore, the unique characteristics of the high-altitude environment may drive variations in metabolic functions, oxygen tolerance, and energy acquisition in different bacteria. To explore the potential impacts of these alterations in gut microbiota, PICRUSt analysis was employed to predict variations in metabolic functions of the gut microbial community; the main differential metabolic pathway of Han populations with different altitudes is lipid metabolism (Fig.
5
E).

A comparable investigation was conducted on the microbiota of Han and Tibetan populations living at high altitudes.
Bacteroidota
and
Firmicutes
had the highest relative abundance (Supplemental Fig. 4 A). The α-diversity and β-diversity analyses revealed significant differences in species richness, evenness, and community evenness between high-altitude Han and Tibetan populations (Supplemental Fig. 4B and C). High-altitude Han individuals had a much higher abundance of multiple genera, including
Prevotella_9
, but
Subdoligranulum
,
Blautia
, and
Fusicatenibacter
abundance was dramatically lower (Supplemental Fig. 4D). Tibetan populations also exhibited significant differences in lipid metabolism pathways, with increased activity in carbohydrate, lipid, and amino acid metabolism pathways compared to high-altitude Han individuals (Supplemental Fig. 5).
Relationship between serum metabolites, clinical indicators, and gut microbiota
To better understand the potential influence of the gut microbiota on the host plasma metabolome, we integrated data from the fecal microbiome and plasma metabolomics to identify microbial communities strongly associated with specific plasma compounds. We first conducted Weighted Gene Co-expression Network Analysis (WGCNA) with the plasma metabolomics data. Since no outliers or visible clusters were detected with the hierarchical clustering, then the analysis with a soft threshold (power of
β
= 4) was performed to reduce noise and enhance the formation of distinct clusters in the final network. WGCNA identified 5 and 7 broad-target and lipid metabolites modules in the plain and plateau Han populations, respectively (Supplemental Fig. 6 A, B). Additionally, WGCNA identified 6 broad-target and lipid metabolites modules in the Han and Tibetan plateau populations, respectively (Supplemental Fig. 6 C, D).

We then explored the connection between the KEGG modules from the microbiome and metabolites with the Spearman correlation coefficients. In the plain and plateau Han populations, the heatmap revealed significant connections, with b_ME1, l_ME5, l_ME4, and l_ME3 metabolite modules showing strong correlations with multiple KO pathways (Fig.
6
A). These modules predominantly contained lipids and nucleotides, which had significant negative associations with microbial metabolic pathways, including aspartate and glutamate metabolism, purine metabolism, and pyrimidine metabolism. Conversely, they exhibited strong positive associations with tryptophan metabolism, phenylalanine metabolism, and various other metabolic pathways (Fig.
6
A). In the high-altitude Han-Tibetan community, notable negative associations were observed between metabolites and steroid breakdown, along with strong positive associations with pathways related to aspartate and glutamate metabolism (Fig.
6
B). This integrative analysis highlighted significant correlations between gut microbial communities and plasma metabolites, particularly linking lipid and nucleotide metabolism with key pathways such as purine, pyrimidine, and amino acid metabolism, underscoring the role of gut microbiota in high-altitude adaptation (Supplemental Fig. 7).
Discussion
Our study comprehensively analyzes the effects of high altitude on metabolism and gut microbiota across different ethnicities and altitudes. Previous studies have often focused on a single ethnicity or region and utilized metabolomics or gut microbiota analysis alone, lacking an integrative approach [
1
,
19
,
20
]. For instance, it has been shown that hypoxia at high altitudes leads to significant changes in lipid metabolism, including elevated uric acid levels due to increased oxidative stress and alterations in purine metabolism [
1
,
19
,
20
]. To address these gaps, we systematically performed metabolomics and 16S rRNA sequencing analyses on fecal and plasma samples from plain-dwelling Han, high-altitude Han, and high-altitude Tibetan populations, aiming to identify differences in metabolites, microbial communities, and co-metabolic pathways. This integrative approach offers a more holistic view of how environmental factors like altitude shape human health across different ethnicities.
Our study reveals significant clinical indicators and metabolic profile differences among plain-dwelling Han, high-altitude Han, and high-altitude Tibetan populations. The high-altitude Han population exhibited distinct metabolic and hormonal profiles, with elevated levels of lipase, insulin, and glucose, and reduced levels of pancreatic amylase and high-density lipoprotein, aligning with previous findings that hypoxia at high altitudes alters energy metabolism and lipid processing [
1
,
11
,
17
,
19
,
21
,
22
]. Differences between high-altitude Han and Tibetan populations, particularly in glucose metabolism and lipid profiles, highlight adaptive modifications these groups have undergone in response to prolonged low-oxygen conditions [
23
,
24
]. Our metabolomics analysis identified distinct signatures among the groups, shedding light on metabolic adaptations to altitude. In high-altitude Han populations, ceramide and hypoxanthine-9-β-D-arabinofuranoside were significantly associated with clinical indicators like urea and LDIP [
25
,
26
], confirming that hypoxia increases oxidative stress and alters purine metabolism, leading to elevated uric acid levels [
9
,
20
,
27
]. Specific lipid metabolites and their associations with clinical markers in the high-altitude Han-Tibetan population point to unique metabolic strategies for coping with altitude-induced stress, potentially through selective lipid utilization and reprogramming of the purine pathway [
6
,
10
,
13
]. The novelty of our study lies in the systematic comparison of multiple ethnic groups and altitudes, revealing how these factors interact to produce diverse metabolic profiles.
Our findings revealed significant differences in gut microbiota composition among the groups, closely related to variations in plasma metabolomic profiles. High-altitude Han individuals exhibited a higher prevalence of
Prevotella
and
Streptococcus
, alongside a reduced abundance of
Bacteroides
and
Bifidobacterium
, suggesting that gut microbiota play a crucial role in mediating physiological adaptations to altitude [
14
,
28
]. These microbial shifts may facilitate adaptation to hypoxic conditions by modulating metabolic pathways related to energy acquisition, oxygen utilization, and oxidative stress responses. For example,
Prevotella
species degrade complex carbohydrates, enhancing energy extraction from the diet—crucial in low-oxygen environments with high metabolic demands [
29
,
30
]. Increased abundance of
Streptococcus
may contribute to the production of short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs), which modulate host energy metabolism and inflammatory responses [
2
,
3
,
31
], while certain gut bacteria produce metabolites like glutathione and other antioxidant compounds that neutralize reactive oxygen species, protecting against hypoxia-induced oxidative damage [
9
,
20
,
32
]. Comparing high-altitude Han and Tibetan populations, we observed notable differences in microbial composition, with Tibetans exhibiting higher richness and diversity indices. This greater microbial diversity may enhance metabolic flexibility, allowing Tibetans to extract and utilize nutrients more effectively under hypoxic conditions [
5
,
7
,
33
]. The enriched metabolic pathways in the Tibetan gut microbiota included carbohydrate, lipid, and amino acid metabolism pathways, linked to metabolites involved in energy metabolism, oxygen transport, and protection against oxidative stress, all crucial for high-altitude survival. Our metabolomics analysis identified specific metabolites significantly associated with the gut microbiota in Tibetans, such as DL-2-aminooctanoic acid, deoxycholic acid, hyodeoxycholic acid, and triglycerides. Deoxycholic and hyodeoxycholic acids, bile acids derived from microbial metabolism, influence lipid digestion and modulate host metabolic processes via receptors like FXR and TGR5 [
34
,
35
]. The integration of metabolomics and microbiota data highlighted significant correlations between metabolite modules containing lipids and nucleotides and microbial pathways related to amino acid metabolism, suggesting that the gut microbiota enhances amino acid biosynthesis, hormonal balance, and antioxidant defenses under hypoxic stress [
36
,
37
].
In conclusion, by integrating metabolomics and microbiota data, our study highlights the complex interplay between host metabolism and microbial communities in response to altitude, providing a comprehensive understanding of high-altitude adaptation. Our integrated approach addresses a critical gap in our understanding of human adaptation to extreme environments and offers potential intervention targets for preventing and treating altitude-related diseases. These findings have significant implications for personalized medicine and public health interventions in high-altitude regions, where therapeutic strategies targeting the gut microbiome, such as probiotics or dietary modifications, could enhance metabolic efficiency and resilience to hypoxia-related stress, guiding the development of strategies to mitigate altitude-related health risks in diverse populations.
Conclusions
This study is the first to integrate metabolomic and microbiomic analyses to explore metabolic and microbial adaptations across different ethnic groups in different environments. We found significant differences in lipid and purine metabolism between plateau Han, plain Han, and Tibetan populations, highlighting the unique adaptive strategies of these groups in response to hypoxia. Notably, the gut microbiota composition and function showed substantial changes, particularly in lipid, carbohydrate, and amino acid metabolism, suggesting these pathways play a key role in high-altitude adaptation. This research provides new insights into the mechanisms of high-altitude adaptation and offers potential microbiome-targeted interventions for preventing and treating altitude-related health issues, holding significant medical and public health value.
Methods
Study cohort
We carefully designed the experiment and recruitment criteria, and recruited a total of 349 healthy Han Chinese and Tibetan Chinese residents, of which 94 Han Chinese lived in the plain at an average altitude of 1200 m and had never been to the plateau; 162 Han Chinese and 93 Tibetans lived in the plateau at an average altitude of 4300 m, and the Han Chinese had been working in the plateau for more than 3 months, and this was their first time going there. 93 Tibetans had always lived on the plateau and had never been to the plain. All the samples of the plain-living population were collected on the plain, and all the samples of the plateau-living population were collected on the plateau. The Han and Tibetan populations on the plateau have roughly similar diets and lifestyles; they live in the same cafeteria and eat traditional Chinese food in the same cafeteria, and the plain populations have similar lifestyles and diets to those on the plateau. Thus, this design largely eliminated some confounders (diet and lifestyle), with the main factors being ethnicity and altitude differences. All participants were healthy, had no known clinical illnesses, and were not taking medications or receiving any interventions during the plateau. See supplemental data 1 in the supplementary material for raw data statistics.
Collection of blood and fecal samples, biochemistry tests
In the morning when participants were fasting, 8 ml of anticoagulated blood was collected using EDTA-K2, mixed by gentle up and down mixing, centrifuged using a centrifugation speed of 4000 rpm for 10 min, and the supernatant (200 µL) was then transferred into a 1.5-mL centrifuge tube for untargeted metabolomics analysis using LC–MS/MS. Plasma samples were separated and transported to the PLA General Hospital (Beijing, approximately 40 m above sea level) while maintaining − 80 °C temperature throughout transit to ensure sample stability. Two milliliters of plasma were taken for 76 clinical parameters using a hematology analyzer (Roche, USA), and the supernatant was taken for metabolite assays, all of which were performed by Metware Biotechnology (Wuhan, China), and all the blood tests and basic statistical descriptions are detailed in supplemental data 1. Fresh fecal samples were collected using a sterile fecal collector. The middle portion of the sample was then taken using a sterile fecal sampler. Each fecal sample was weighed at approximately 0.2 g and dispensed into a new 1.5-mL centrifuge tube. Each sample collected is transferred to − 80 °C within 20 min for storage.
Sample preparation and extraction
16S rRNA gene sequencing. Fecal specimens were extracted using the standard method of Novogene (Beijing, China), and PCR was performed to amplify the V3–V4 region of the 16S rRNA gene using the 341F/806R primers. We mixed the amplification products with 1 × loading buffer containing SYBR green fluorescent dye in equal volumes, and then prepared sequencing libraries according to the manufacturer’s protocol for the Ion Plus Fragment Library Kit 48rxns from Thermo Scientific (USA). We chose to perform high-throughput sequencing on the Ion S5 XL platform and obtained approximately 400 bp of single-ended raw reads from each sample.
Metabolite assay
In this study, metabolite analysis was performed using the Metware Metabolic Assay System, where liquid samples were first prepared and extracted; hydrophilic compounds were mixed by 20% acetonitrile-methanol internal standard extracts and the supernatant was obtained by centrifugation, whereas hydrophobic compounds were processed by methyl tert-butyl ether (MTBE): MeOH extracts. Then, the hydrophilic and hydrophobic compounds were analyzed separately by UPLC technique, where the hydrophilic compounds were analyzed by two UPLC conditions including T3 and Amide, and the hydrophobic compounds were analyzed by UPLC conditions involving a C30 column. Finally, the hydrophilic and hydrophobic compounds were analyzed by ESI-Q TRAP-MS/MS mass spectrometry system, and the metabolite data were obtained by using LIT and QQQ scanning modes, which provided an effective means of revealing the in-depth composition and abundance of metabolites in the samples.
Analytical methods
Analysis of clinical indicators
We used the shapiro.test function in the
R
statistical package, which was used to perform the Shapiro–Wilk normality test on the clinical indicator data, with the
p
-value cutoff set at 0.05. To compare the differences in normally distributed variables between the two groups, we used an independent
t
-test. For the assessment of differences between non-normally distributed data, we instead chose the Wilcoxon test. To correct for multiple comparisons, we applied the Benjamini–Hochberg procedure to control the false discovery rate (FDR). This approach was used to adjust p-values for all tests conducted in the study to minimize the risk of Type I errors due to multiple testing. The
p
-values were adjusted using the Benjamini–Hochberg procedure with a false discovery rate threshold of 0.05.
Identification of differential metabolites
We applied the Wilcoxon test using the Wilcox.test function in the R package, with the
p
-value set to 0.05 to identify metabolites showing significant differences between groups. In addition, we also relied on the RandomForest method, which was performed by the “randomForest” function in the R package “randomForest” to build the model. The model performance was evaluated with the help of the predict function for the test dataset and the multiclass.roc function to calculate the AUC value to evaluate the model performance. To identify the most influential metabolites, we calculated the importance of model variables and selected the top 30 metabolites based on their variable importance scores. In addition, we used the OPLS-DA method and grouped principal component analysis, which was performed using the R package “ropls”. In the determination of significantly different metabolites, we relied on the criteria VIP ≥ 1 and absolute Log2FC ≥ 1. These thresholds were chosen as they are widely used in metabolomics studies to identify variables with the highest discrimination power between groups. Prior to the application of the above methods, we performed logarithmic transformation (log2) on all metabolic data. For cluster analysis, we used the R package “ComplexHeatmap” for cluster analysis of samples and differential metabolites, and the R package “glasso” for the analysis of differential metabolites and clinical indicators.
Microbiome analysis
For high-throughput sequencing data analysis, we used the R package DADA2. Sequences were demultiplexed, and non-biological nucleotides (primers, adapters) were removed using cutadapt (v5.1). Low-quality bases were filtered and corrected, and ASVs were generated using DADA2 (v1.26), which includes sequence dereplication, error correction, and chimera removal. Taxonomy was assigned using the assignTaxonomy function in DADA2, which employs a naive Bayesian classifier based on
k
-mer frequency to assign taxonomic affiliations across multiple taxonomic ranks. The sequences were compared to the SILVA v138.2 database, and only bacterial ASVs were retained for downstream analysis. On this basis, we retained only bacterial sequence variants (ASVs) and filtered out sequences from other domains. Compositional and functional analysis of the microbiome was performed using the R package “phyloseq,” involving filtering of low-frequency sequence variants, removal of unclassified phyla, and normalization of ASV abundance. At the same time, we performed α-diversity analysis and β-diversity analysis based on diversity indices such as Chao1, Shannon, Simpson, and ACE, respectively, and also used β-diversity analysis based on Unweighted-UniFrac distance. For microbiome function analysis, we used the PiCRUST2 software to predict microbiome functions and to estimate the involvement of microorganisms in different functional pathways. For differential abundance analysis of microbiome functions, we used the R software packages “ggpicrust2” and “MaAsLin2” to reveal the correlation between microbiome and clinical data.
KEGG annotation and enrichment analysis
To annotate the metabolites identified by the 3 methods, we used the KEGG Compound database. Subsequently, we mapped the annotated metabolites to the KEGG Pathway database to identify significantly enriched pathways; we applied the
p
-value of the hypergeometric test. This step aims to perform pathway enrichment analysis for a given list of metabolites.
